claim: Yeast tRNA ligase (Trl1) is an essential trifunctional enzyme that catalyzes exon-exon ligation during tRNA biogenesis and the non-conventional splicing of HAC1 mRNA during the unfolded protein response (UPR).
source: Yeast tRNA ligase (Trl1) is an essential trifunctional enzyme that catalyzes exon-exon ligation during tRNA biogenesis and the non-conventional splicing of HAC1 mRNA during the unfolded protein response (UPR).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript to prior work establishing these functions.

claim: The crystal structure of Trl1 RNA ligase domain from Chaetomium thermophilum was solved at 1.9 Å resolution.
source: Here we report the crystal structure of Trl1 RNA ligase domain from Chaetomium thermophilum at 1.9 Å resolution.
evidence: The resolution is stated in the abstract and confirmed in the data collection statistics table (Table 1).

claim: Structure-based mutational analyses uncovered kinetic competition between RNA ligation and degradation during HAC1 mRNA splicing.
source: Structure-based mutational analyses uncovered kinetic competition between RNA ligation and degradation during HAC1 mRNA splicing.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that deletion of RNA decay pathways rescues the trl1-H148Y mutant phenotype (Figures 5 and 6).

claim: Incompletely processed HAC1 mRNA is degraded by Xrn1 and the Ski/exosome complex.
source: Incompletely processed HAC1 mRNA is degraded by Xrn1 and the Ski/exosome complex.
evidence: This is demonstrated by genetic experiments showing that deletion of XRN1 or SKI2 rescues the trl1-H148Y mutant (Figure 5B).

claim: Cleaved HAC1 mRNA is an endogenous substrate for ribosome-associated quality control.
source: We establish cleaved HAC1 mRNA as endogenous substrate for ribosome-associated quality control.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that deletion of DOM34 re-sensitizes ski2Δ trl1-H148Y cells to ER stress (Figure 6A) and by detection of ubiquitinated Hac1 truncated protein (Figure 6B).

claim: Trl1 is a tripartite enzyme consisting of an N-terminal adenylyltransferase domain (ligase; LIG), a C-terminal cyclic phosphodiesterase domain (CPD) and a central polynucleotide kinase (KIN) domain.
source: Trl1 is a tripartite enzyme (Figure 1A), consisting of an N-terminal adenylyltransferase domain (ligase; LIG), which belongs to the nucleotidyltransferase superfamily alongside DNA ligases and RNA capping enzymes, a C-terminal cyclic phosphodiesterase domain (CPD) and a central polynucleotide kinase (KIN) domain (Phizicky et al., 1986; Xu et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to prior work and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Trl1 substrates initially contain a 2',3' cyclic phosphate and a 5'-OH group at the RNA termini.
source: Trl1 substrates initially contain a 2',3' cyclic phosphate and a 5'-OH group at the RNA termini (Greer et al., 1983).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work by Greer et al., 1983.

claim: The CPD activity opens the 2',3' cyclic phosphate by hydrolysis to form a 3'-OH/2' phosphate terminus.
source: First, the CPD activity opens the 2',3' cyclic phosphate by hydrolysis to form a 3'-OH/2' phosphate terminus
evidence: This is described in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B showing the mechanism.

claim: The KIN activity phosphorylates the 5'-OH in an NTP-dependent reaction, preferring GTP over ATP.
source: and, second, the KIN activity phosphorylates the 5'-OH in an NTP-dependent reaction – preferring GTP over ATP.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the ligation mechanism and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The LIG activity 'seals' the healed ends through ATP-dependent phosphodiester bond formation.
source: Third, the LIG activity 'seals' the healed ends through ATP-dependent phosphodiester bond formation.
evidence: This is described in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The ligation reaction occurs in three nucleotidyl transfer steps: (1) Trl1-LIG reacts with ATP to form a covalent LIG-(lysyl-N)-AMP intermediate; (2) the bound AMP is transferred to the 5' phosphate end to form a 5'-to-5' RNA-adenylate; (3) Trl1-LIG catalyzes the attack by the 3'-OH on the RNA-adenylate to form a phosphodiester bond, releasing AMP.
source: This final reaction occurs in three nucleotidyl transfer steps: (1) Trl1-LIG reacts with ATP to form a covalent LIG-(lysyl-N)-AMP intermediate; (2) the bound AMP is transferred to the 5' phosphate end to form a 5'-to-5' RNA-adenylate; (3) Trl1-LIG catalyzes the attack by the 3'-OH on the RNA-adenylate to form a phosphodiester bond, releasing AMP (Greer et al., 1983; Phizicky et al., 1986).
evidence: This mechanism is described with citations and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The remaining 2' phosphate at the splice junction is removed by Tpt1, a 2' phosphotransferase that is essential for cell viability.
source: The remaining 2' phosphate at the splice junction is removed by an additional enzyme, Tpt1, which is a 2' phosphotransferase that, like Trl1, is also essential for cell viability (Banerjee et al., 2019; Culver et al., 1997; Culver et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Trl1 ligates tRNA halves after intron excision by the tRNA splicing endonuclease (SEN) complex.
source: Trl1 ligates tRNA halves after intron excision by the tRNA splicing endonuclease (SEN) complex (Greer et al., 1983; Peebles et al., 1983).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Trl1 is a key component of the UPR, a major intracellular stress signaling pathway.
source: In addition, it is a key component of the UPR, a major intracellular stress signaling pathway (Sidrauski et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated with citation to the original discovery paper.

claim: The UPR regulates the protein folding capacity of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: All eukaryotic cells monitor and adjust the protein folding capacity of their endoplasmic reticulum (ER) through the UPR signaling network.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about the UPR.

claim: Protein folding stress in the ER activates the cytosolic endonuclease domain of the transmembrane stress sensor Ire1.
source: Protein folding stress in the ER activates the cytosolic endonuclease domain of the transmembrane stress sensor Ire1 (Cox et al., 1993; Mori et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The activated RNase cleaves HAC1 mRNA in fungi or XBP1 mRNA in metazoans at the splice sites.
source: The activated RNase cleaves HAC1 mRNA in fungi or XBP1 mRNA in metazoans at the splice sites (Calfon et al., 2002; Cox and Walter, 1996; Yoshida et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: A conformational change within the RNA actively ejects the intron and coordinates the two exons.
source: Next, a conformational change within the RNA actively ejects the intron and coordinates the two exons (Gonzalez et al., 1999; Peschek et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The exons are ligated by Trl1 in fungi or the RTCB ligase complex in metazoans.
source: which are ligated by Trl1 in fungi (Sidrauski et al., 1996) or the RTCB ligase complex in metazoans (Jurkin et al., 2014; Kosmaczewski et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The spliced HAC1 and XBP1 mRNAs are translated to produce the active transcription factors Hac1 and XBP1 that drive expression of UPR target genes.
source: The spliced HAC1 and XBP1 mRNAs are then translated to produce the active transcription factors Hac1 and XBP1 that drive expression of UPR target genes in yeast and metazoan cells, respectively (Cox and Walter, 1996; Mori et al., 1996; Nikawa et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: A yeast genetic screen in Saccharomyces cerevisiae revealed a single His(148)Tyr point mutation within Trl1-LIG that abolished the UPR signaling in vivo yet did not impair tRNA splicing.
source: Intriguingly, a yeast genetic screen in Saccharomyces cerevisiae (sc) revealed a single His(148)Tyr point mutation lying within Trl1-LIG that in vivo abolished the UPR signaling yet did not impair tRNA splicing. This mutant allele (henceforth referred to as trl1-H148Y, originally named rlg1-100) paved the way to discovery of Trl1 as the RNA ligase during Ire1-mediated splicing of HAC1 mRNA (Sidrauski et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated with citation to the original discovery paper.

claim: ctTrl1 has the same tripartite domain structure as scTrl1 with 39% overall sequence identity.
source: ctTrl1 has the same tripartite domain structure as scTrl1 (Figure 1A) with 39% overall sequence identity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expression of ctTrl1 rescued S. cerevisiae trl1∆ cells from the lethal effects of the deletion, both under normal growth conditions as well as during ER stress induced by tunicamycin.
source: Moreover, expression of ctTrl1 rescued S. cerevisiae trl1∆ cells from the lethal effects of the deletion, both under normal growth conditions as well as during ER stress induced by tunicamycin (Tm), an inhibitor of N-linked glycosylation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the growth assay shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ctTrl1 catalyzes in S. cerevisiae cells the ligation of both tRNA halves, thus sustaining normal growth, and HAC1 mRNA exons during the UPR.
source: Hence, ctTrl1 catalyzes in S. cerevisiae cells the ligation of both tRNA halves, thus sustaining normal growth, and HAC1 mRNA exons during the UPR.
evidence: This is inferred from the complementation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Recombinantly expressed ctTrl1 efficiently ligated the exons of a HAC1-derived RNA substrate after its endonucleolytic cleavage by Ire1 in vitro.
source: In addition, recombinantly expressed ctTrl1 efficiently ligated the exons of a HAC1-derived RNA substrate, HAC1U-508 ('U' for unspliced, that is intron containing), after its endonucleolytic cleavage by Ire1 completing the splicing reaction in vitro (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the in vitro splicing assay shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The overall structure of ctTrl1-LIG delineates two subdomains: an N-terminal (LIG-N; aa 13–326) and a C-terminal (LIG-C; aa 327–407) subdomain.
source: The overall structure delineates two subdomains: an N-terminal (LIG-N; aa 13–326) and a C-terminal (LIG-C; aa 327–407) subdomain (Figure 3A, colored blue and yellow, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: LIG-N is composed of three central antiparallel β-sheets surrounded by seven α-helices.
source: LIG-N is composed of three central antiparallel β-sheets surrounded by seven α-helices.
evidence: This is a description of the crystal structure.

claim: The overall architecture of the LIG-N domain resembles the bacteriophage T4 RNA ligase (T4Rnl1) structure consistent with it carrying the adenylyltransferase activity.
source: The overall architecture of this domain resembles the bacteriophage T4 RNA ligase (T4Rnl1) structure consistent with it carrying the adenylyltransferase activity (El Omari et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior structural work on T4Rnl1.

claim: LIG-C has an all-helical fold that is unrelated to all other structures in the PDB from the same superfamily based on structural comparison by Dali.
source: LIG-C has an all-helical fold that is unrelated, based on structural comparison by Dali (Holm and Laakso, 2016), to all other structures in the PDB from the same superfamily, which besides ATP-dependent RNA ligases also includes DNA ligases and mRNA capping enzymes.
evidence: This is stated based on structural comparison using the Dali server.

claim: LIG's active site is buried in the center of a positively charged cleft that spans LIG-N and is extended by LIG-C.
source: LIG's active site is buried in the center of a positively charged cleft that spans LIG-N and is extended by LIG-C (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the electrostatic surface potential map in Figure 3B.

claim: The adenosine nucleotide binding pocket is contained in LIG-N.
source: The adenosine nucleotide binding pocket is contained in LIG-N.
evidence: This is stated based on the crystal structure.

claim: In the structure, Nζ of Lys148 is more than 4 Å away from the α-phosphonate, suggestive of conformational rearrangements necessary for the formation of the Trl1-(lysyl-N)-AMP intermediate.
source: In our structure, Nζ of Lys148 in the highly conserved nucleotide binding motif I [Kx(D/H/N)G] (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which is the site of covalent AMP attachment, is more than 4 Å away from the α-phosphonate (Figure 3C), suggestive of conformational rearrangements necessary for the formation of the Trl1-(lysyl-N)-AMP intermediate.
evidence: This is stated based on analysis of the crystal structure shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Thr146, Leu147, Glu149, Arg305 and Lys325 form contacts with the adenine base via hydrogen bonding, and His241 via π-stacking.
source: Thr146, Leu147, Glu149, Arg305 and Lys325 form contacts with the adenine base via hydrogen bonding, and His241 via π-stacking.
evidence: This is stated based on analysis of the crystal structure and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The adenosine nucleoside base of AMPcPP is in syn conformation.
source: The adenosine nucleoside base of AMPcPP is in syn conformation.
evidence: This is stated based on analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: Arg99 functions as hydrogen bond donor with the 3' oxygen of the ribose ring and together with Lys169 forms salt-bridges to the γ-phosphate.
source: Arg99 functions as hydrogen bond donor with the 3' oxygen of the ribose ring and together with Lys169 forms salt-bridges to the γ-phosphate (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated based on analysis of the crystal structure shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Two conserved residues, Arg334 and Arg337, within an α-helix (α11) of the LIG-C subdomain coordinate a single well-ordered sulfate ion via salt bridges near the active site pocket.
source: Two conserved residues, Arg334 and Arg337, within an α-helix (α11) of the LIG-C subdomain coordinate a single well-ordered sulfate ion via salt bridges near the active site pocket.
evidence: This is stated based on analysis of the crystal structure and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: His227 is within distance to form a third salt bridge with the sulfate ion, and Asn150 forms a hydrogen bond with the sulfate ion.
source: In addition, His227 is within distance to form a third salt bridge, and Asn150 forms a hydrogen bond with the sulfate ion (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated based on analysis of the crystal structure shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Arg337 and His227 have been previously identified as essential residues by alanine scanning mutagenesis.
source: Notably, Arg337 and His227 have been previously identified as essential residues by alanine scanning mutagenesis (Wang and Shuman, 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: The sulfate ion represents a surrogate for one of the phosphate groups of Trl1's RNA substrate.
source: We surmise that the sulfate ion represents a surrogate for one of the phosphate groups of Trl1's RNA substrate.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the position of the sulfate ion in the active site.

claim: All residues previously identified to be essential for the RNA ligase activity of scTrl1 are conserved between S. cerevisiae and C. thermophilum Trl1.
source: Based on the strong homology of S. cerevisiae and C. thermophilum Trl1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), we found all residues previously identified to be essential for the RNA ligase activity of scTrl1 conserved between both species.
evidence: This is stated based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: All essential residues cluster around the active site and are surface exposed.
source: When we mapped these residues on the structure of ctTrl1-LIG (Figure 4A), we found that they all cluster around the active site. In addition, these residues are all surface exposed, which points to their importance to binding and correct positioning of RNA substrates.
evidence: This is stated based on mapping residues onto the crystal structure shown in Figure 4A.

claim: His148 was identified as an essential residue as its change to Ala, Asn, or Gln scored as lethal in vivo.
source: Interestingly, His148 was also identified as an essential residue as its change to Ala, Asn, or Gln scored as lethal in vivo (Wang and Shuman, 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Cells bearing the sc-trl1-H148Y allele were viable and shown previously to block UPR-induced nonconventional mRNA splicing.
source: By contrast, cells bearing the sc-trl1-H148Y allele were viable and shown previously to block UPR-induced nonconventional mRNA splicing (Sidrauski et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: His182 in ctTrl1 (equivalent to His148 in scTrl1) is surface-exposed and located on the periphery of the active-site groove in the vicinity of other essential residues.
source: This conserved histidine (His182 in ctTrl1) is surface-exposed and located on the periphery of the active-site groove in the vicinity of other essential residues (Figure 4A, colored red).
evidence: This is stated based on analysis of the crystal structure shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Equivalent concentrations of the WT enzyme yielded more spliced product of the HAC1U-508 RNA substrate compared to scTrl1-LIG-H148Y.
source: Equivalent concentrations of the WT enzyme yielded more spliced (i.e. ligated) product of the HAC1U-508 RNA substrate compared to scTrl1-LIG-H148Y (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the in vitro ligation assay shown in Figure 4B.

claim: scTrl1-H148Y is catalytically impaired towards a HAC1-derived RNA substrate but not inactive.
source: These results indicate that scTrl1-H148Y is catalytically impaired towards a HAC1-derived RNA substrate but not inactive.
evidence: This is concluded from the in vitro ligation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The H148Y mutation has only a small impact on binding affinity towards HAC1-derived 5' and 3' exon RNA oligonucleotides.
source: Despite the reduced ligation efficiency of the H148Y mutant, we only observed a small impact on binding affinity towards the RNA substrates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated based on fluorescence titration experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The H148Y mutant has a 2.2-fold longer half-life (t1/2 = 9.2 min) compared to WT ligase (t1/2 = 4.1 min) in RNA oligonucleotide ligation assays.
source: The results were fitted to a first-order model (Figure 4D) and revealed a 2.2-fold longer half-life for the H148Y mutant (t1/2 = 9.2 min) compared to WT ligase (t1/2 = 4.1 min).
evidence: This is stated based on kinetic analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The mutant ligase plateaued at a lower amount of ligation product (8%) compared to wild-type enzyme (50%).
source: Interestingly, the mutant ligase did not only display slower ligation kinetics but also plateaued at a lower amount of ligation product (8%) compared to wild-type enzyme (50%).
evidence: This is stated based on the kinetic data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Expression of scTrl1-H148Y and ctTrl1-H182Y from the strong constitutive ADH1 promoter allowed growth on tunicamycin-containing medium.
source: To test this notion directly, we expressed Trl1-H148Y from the strong constitutive alcohol dehydrogenase 1 (ADH1) promoter. Both scTrl1-H148Y and ctTrl1-H182Y allowed growth on Tm-containing medium, as did expression of the corresponding LIG only construct (Figure 5A, compare sector 1 to 2 and 4, and sector 1 to 3 and 5, respectively).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the growth assay shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The suppression of the mutant phenotype by overexpression emphasizes that the His148-to-Tyr mutation does not fully inhibit Trl1-LIG functionality and that it is the reduced enzymatic activity of the LIG domain only that becomes limiting.
source: The suppression of the mutant phenotype emphasizes that the His148-to-Tyr mutation does not fully inhibit Trl1-LIG functionality and that it is indeed the reduced enzymatic activity of the LIG domain only that becomes limiting, causing the UPR-deficient phenotype of trl1-H148Y cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the overexpression rescue data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Individual deletion of either XRN1 or SKI2 rescued growth of trl1-H148Y cells upon ER stress.
source: Indeed, individual deletion of either XRN1 or SKI2 rescued growth of trl1-H148Y cells upon ER stress (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the growth assay shown in Figure 5B.

claim: xrn1Δ cells exhibited a reduced colony size, which might be explained by the annotated slow growth phenotype of XRN1 deletion being exacerbated in the presence of ER stress.
source: While growth of ski2Δ cells was indistinguishable from that of WT cells, xrn1Δ cells exhibited a reduced colony size, which might be explained by the annotated slow growth phenotype of XRN1 deletion being exacerbated in the presence of ER stress.
evidence: This is stated based on observation of the growth assay in Figure 5B.

claim: Neither the xrn1Δ hac1Δ nor the ski2Δ hac1Δ strain were viable in the presence of ER stress.
source: To ensure that the observed rescue indeed resulted from restored UPR signaling, we generated HAC1 deletions in the respective strains and tested their growth. Neither the xrn1Δ hac1Δ nor the ski2Δ hac1Δ strain were viable in the presence of ER stress (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the growth assay shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The rescue by deletion of the major cytosolic RNA degradation pathway in either the 5'-to-3' or the 3'-to-5' direction substantiates that non-conventional splicing and RNA decay are competing outcomes after Ire1 cleavage of HAC1 mRNA.
source: The rescue by deletion of the major cytosolic RNA degradation pathway in either the 5'-to-3' or the 3'-to-5' direction substantiates that non-conventional splicing and RNA decay are competing outcomes after Ire1 cleavage of HAC1 mRNA.
evidence: This is concluded from the genetic rescue data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: HAC1 mRNA was spliced upon Tm-induced ER stress in the WT strain and not affected by deletion of XRN1 or SKI2.
source: As expected, HAC1 mRNA was spliced upon Tm-induced ER stress in the WT strain and not affected by deletion of XRN1 or SKI2 (Figure 5D, lanes 1–6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Upon ER stress, an overall reduction of unspliced HAC1 mRNA and no HAC1 mRNA splicing was detected in trl1-H148Y cells.
source: In agreement with previous results, upon ER stress we detected an overall reduction of unspliced HAC1 mRNA and no HAC1 mRNA splicing in trl1-H148Y cells (Figure 5D, lanes 7 and 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Deletion of XRN1 in trl1-H148Y cells restored splicing, albeit not to the same degree as in the WT strain.
source: Deletion of XRN1 in trl1-H148Y cells restored splicing, albeit not to the same degree as in the WT strain (Figure 5D, lanes 11 and 12).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Stabilization of the severed HAC1 3' exon in the absence of Xrn1 allows enzymatically impaired Trl1-H148Y to catch up and ligate the HAC1 exons to restore the UPR.
source: We surmise that stabilization of the severed HAC1 3' exon in the absence of the major 5'-to-3' exonuclease Xrn1 allows enzymatically impaired Trl1-H148Y to catch up and ligate the HAC1 exons to restore the UPR.
evidence: This is inferred from the RT-PCR data showing restored splicing in xrn1Δ trl1-H148Y cells (Figure 5D).

claim: No spliced HAC1 mRNA was detected in ski2Δ trl1-H148Y cells upon ER stress, but rather a reduction of unspliced HAC1 mRNA.
source: To our surprise, despite the complete phenotypic rescue shown above (Figure 5B), we did not detect spliced HAC1 mRNA in ski2Δ trl1-H148Y cells upon ER stress (Figure 5D, lanes 9 and 10), but rather a reduction of unspliced HAC1 mRNA, reminiscent of the parental trl1-H148Y mutant strain.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: When RT-PCR was performed on the 5' exon with cDNA templates from the entire cellular RNA (using random hexamers for priming), an increase in the amount of the HAC1 5' exon was observed upon SKI2 deletion compared to the parental trl1-H148Y strain.
source: Interestingly, when we performed the same RT-PCR on the 5' exon with cDNA templates from the entire cellular RNA (using random hexamers for priming), we now observed an increase in the amount of the HAC1 5' exon upon SKI2 deletion, when compared to the parental trl1-H148Y strain (Figure 5D, row 3, compare lanes 8 and 10).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The genetic ablation of Xrn1 restored HAC1 mRNA splicing in the UPR-deficient yeast cells.
source: The genetic ablation of the major 5'-to-3' exonuclease Xrn1 restored HAC1 mRNA splicing in the UPR-deficient yeast cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Abrogation of cytosolic RNA exosome by disruption of the Ski complex suppressed ER stress sensitivity solely via stabilization of the severed 5' exon.
source: By contrast, as we did not detect spliced HAC1 mRNA in ski2Δ trl1-H148Y cells, abrogation of cytosolic RNA exosome by disruption of the Ski complex must have suppressed ER stress sensitivity solely via stabilization of the severed 5' exon.
evidence: This is concluded from the RT-PCR data showing no spliced HAC1 mRNA but increased 5' exon in ski2Δ trl1-H148Y cells (Figure 5D).

claim: A truncated form of Hac1 produced from an mRNA bearing a stop codon immediately after the 5' exon (Hac1trunc) is a fundamentally still functional transcription factor that can induce the UPR.
source: Previous studies showed that a truncated form of Hac1 produced from an mRNA bearing a stop codon immediately after the 5' exon and hence lacking the entire C-terminal portion encoded by the 3' exon (Hac1trunc) is a fundamentally still functional transcription factor that can induce the UPR (Cox and Walter, 1996; Di Santo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The stabilized, cleaved 5' exon in the ski2Δ trl1-H148Y strain should be subject to co-translational mRNA surveillance by no-go decay (NGD).
source: Since the stabilized, cleaved 5' exon in the ski2Δ trl1-H148Y strain reported here does not contain a stop codon, it should be subject to co-translational mRNA surveillance by no-go decay (NGD).
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that the 5' exon lacks a stop codon.

claim: Deletion of DOM34 re-sensitized ski2Δ trl1-H148Y cells to ER stress.
source: Growth analysis of these strains showed that deletion of DOM34 re-sensitized ski2Δ trl1-H148Y cells to ER stress (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the growth assay shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Rescue of trl1-H148Y by depletion of Ski2 is dependent on successful ribosome rescue at the 5' non-conventional splice site of the cleaved HAC1 mRNA.
source: Thus, rescue of trl1-H148Y by depletion of Ski2 (i.e. cytosolic RNA exosome activity) is dependent on successful ribosome rescue at the 5' non-conventional splice site of the cleaved HAC1 mRNA.
evidence: This is concluded from the DOM34 deletion data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Hac1 was produced upon ER stress in WT cells and absent in trl1-H148Y cells.
source: We confirmed the production of Hac1 upon ER stress in WT cells and the lack of its expression in trl1-H148Y cells (Figure 6B, lanes 1–2 and 9–10).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Full-length Hac1 was detected in xrn1Δ trl1-H148Y cells upon ER stress induction.
source: As expected from the results shown above, upon ER stress induction we detected full-length Hac1 in xrn1Δ trl1-H148Y cells (Figure 6B, lane 12).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The expression levels of Hac1 in xrn1Δ trl1-H148Y cells were lower than in WT cells, in accordance with the reduced amount of spliced HAC1 mRNA produced in this strain.
source: The expression levels were lower than in WT cells, in accordance with the reduced amount of spliced HAC1 mRNA produced in this strain (Figure 5D, compare lane 2 with lane 12).
evidence: This is stated based on comparison of immunoblot and RT-PCR data.

claim: No full-length Hac1 was detected in ski2Δ trl1-H148Y cells exposed to ER stress, but a faster migrating band consistent with a C-terminally truncated form of Hac1 was observed.
source: By contrast, while we detected no Hac1 in ski2Δ trl1-H148Y cells exposed to ER stress, we saw instead a faster migrating band (Figure 6B, lane 14), consistent with the expression of a C-terminally truncated form of Hac1 in these cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A series of higher molecular mass smeared out bands, presumably resulting from ubiquitination, was detected in ski2Δ trl1-H148Y cells.
source: In the same strain, we also detected a series of higher molecular mass smeared out bands, presumably a banding pattern resulting from ubiquitination.
evidence: This is stated based on immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Deletion of SKI2 in the wild-type strain led to an accumulation of truncated Hac1 and higher molecular mass laddering, albeit to a lesser extent than in the respective trl1-H148Y strain.
source: Interestingly, deletion of SKI2 in the wild-type strain also led to an accumulation of truncated Hac1 and higher molecular mass laddering, albeit to a lesser extent than in the respective trl1-H148Y strain.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: RNA decay and ribosome-associated mRNA surveillance play an important role in maintaining the fidelity of HAC1 mRNA splicing in wild-type cells.
source: This result indicated that RNA decay and ribosome-associated mRNA surveillance, while their effects are exacerbated in the UPR mutant strain, play an important role in maintaining the fidelity of HAC1 mRNA splicing in wild-type cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation of truncated Hac1 in ski2Δ WT cells (Figure 6B).

claim: The crystal structure of Trl1-LIG from C. thermophilum revealed a two-domain architecture comprised of a canonical adenylyltransferase domain and a C-terminal domain with a unique all-helical fold within the same enzyme superfamily.
source: The crystal structure of Trl1-LIG from C. thermophilum revealed a two-domain architecture comprised of a canonical adenylyltransferase domain and a C-terminal domain with a unique all-helical fold within the same enzyme superfamily.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the structural data presented.

claim: The C-terminal domain of T4Rnl1 is not required to catalyze RNA ligation but confers specificity for tRNA repair.
source: Previous structural and enzymatic data on T4Rnl1 showed that its C-terminal domain is not required to catalyze RNA ligation but confers specificity for tRNA repair (El Omari et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: The C-terminal domain of ctTrl1-LIG likely confers substrate specificity.
source: Based on these observations and the structural similarities between the adenylyltransferase domains of ctTrl1-LIG and T4Rnl1, we suspect a similar function, that is conferring substrate specificity, of the C-terminal domain of ctTrl1-LIG.
evidence: This is speculated based on comparison with T4Rnl1.

claim: The reduced ligation kinetics of Trl1-H148Y tip the balance almost completely in favor of degrading cleaved HAC1 mRNA.
source: The reduced ligation kinetics of Trl1-H148Y tip the balance almost completely in favor of degrading cleaved HAC1 mRNA.
evidence: This is concluded from the genetic and biochemical data presented.

claim: Both major exonucleolytic decay pathways of the cytosol, Xrn1 and the RNA exosome with the Ski complex, are part of the kinetic competition of RNA processing enzymes during HAC1 mRNA splicing.
source: Both major exonucleolytic decay pathways of the cytosol, Xrn1 and the RNA exosome with the Ski complex, are part of this kinetic competition of RNA processing enzymes, albeit with different roles.
evidence: This is concluded from the genetic rescue experiments shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Xrn1 degrades the 3' exon fragment of cleaved HAC1 and plays an important role in allowing efficient translation from the spliced mRNA.
source: Our data suggest that Xrn1 degrades the 3' exon fragment of cleaved HAC1 and plays an important role in allowing efficient translation from the spliced mRNA.
evidence: This is concluded from the RT-PCR and immunoblot data.

claim: The HAC1 intron in S. cerevisiae blocks translation initiation by forming complementary base pairing with the 5' UTR of the mRNA.
source: The HAC1 intron in S. cerevisiae blocks translation initiation by forming complementary base pairing with the 5' UTR of the mRNA (Rüegsegger et al., 2001; Sathe et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Degradation of the intron after splicing was reported as required for lifting the translational block and the production of Hac1.
source: Degradation of the intron after splicing was reported as required for lifting the translational block and the production of Hac1 (Mori et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Deletion of XRN1, even in the presence of WT Trl1, resulted in lower levels of Hac1 upon ER stress.
source: Deletion of XRN1, even in the presence of WT Trl1, resulted in lower levels of Hac1 upon ER stress.
evidence: This is stated based on immunoblot data.

claim: Xrn1 also degrades tRNA introns during tRNA splicing.
source: Interestingly, Xrn1 also degrades tRNA introns during tRNA splicing, a process with equivalent biochemistry as HAC1 mRNA splicing and shared functionality of Trl1 (Wu and Hopper, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Phosphorylation of the 5' end by Trl1-KIN is required to render the RNA molecules substrates for Xrn1.
source: It should be noted that in all cases phosphorylation of the 5' end, as catalyzed by the central polynucleotide kinase part of Trl1, is required to render the RNA molecules substrates for Xrn1.
evidence: This is stated based on knowledge of Xrn1 substrate requirements.

claim: Kinase-mediated decay poses a permanent competition for Trl1-mediated ligation of any RNA substrate in the cell.
source: In consequence, this kinase-mediated decay poses a permanent competition for Trl1-mediated ligation of any RNA substrate in the cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that Trl1-KIN phosphorylates RNA ends, making them substrates for Xrn1.

claim: Degradation of tRNA introns in yeast has been previously reported to be catalyzed by Trl1-KIN and Xrn1 in an analogous two-step process.
source: Degradation of tRNA introns in yeast has been previously reported to be catalyzed by Trl1-KIN and Xrn1in an analogous two-step process (Wu and Hopper, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Abrogation of the RNA exosome by deletion of SKI2 rescued ER stress sensitivity of trl1-H148Y without restoring splicing, instead by stabilization of the isolated 5' exon fragment of HAC1.
source: We showed that abrogation of the RNA exosome by deletion of SKI2 rescued ER stress sensitivity of trl1-H148Y. However, splicing was not restored in ski2Δ; instead, stabilization of the isolated 5' exon fragment of HAC1 allowed UPR signaling.
evidence: This is concluded from the RT-PCR and growth data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The 18 amino acids encoded in the 3' exon of HAC1 are dispensable for the transactivation function of Hac1p.
source: Previous studies have shown by adding a stop codon after the 5' exon of HAC1 that the 18 amino acids encoded in the 3' exon are dispensable for the transactivation function of Hac1p.
evidence: This is stated with reference to prior work.

claim: Hac1trunc is produced from the isolated HAC1 5' exon in sufficient amounts to initiate the transcriptional response.
source: Indeed, we could demonstrate, that Hac1trunc is produced from the isolated HAC1 5' exon in sufficient amounts to initiate the transcriptional response.
evidence: This is concluded from the growth rescue and immunoblot data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The nascent chain release from the HAC1 5' exon is dependent on ribosome splitting by the NGD pathway.
source: The nascent chain release in this context is dependent on ribosome splitting by the NGD pathway.
evidence: This is concluded from the DOM34 deletion data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: HAC1 mRNA was identified as the strongest Dom34 target by ribosome profiling.
source: This finding is in accordance with a previous study that identified HAC1 mRNA as the strongest Dom34 target by ribosome profiling (Guydosh and Green, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: RIDD in Schizosaccharomyces pombe depends on NGD-mediated ribosome rescue to allow degradation of cleaved mRNAs by the Ski complex/exosome.
source: A recent study demonstrated that RIDD in Schizosaccharomyces pombe also depends on NGD-mediated ribosome rescue to allow degradation of cleaved mRNAs by the Ski complex/exosome (Guydosh et al., 2017; Kimmig et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: NGD plays a crucial role in both functional outputs of the Ire1 branch of the UPR.
source: Together, these findings establish a crucial role of NGD in both functional outputs of the Ire1 branch of the UPR.
evidence: This is concluded from the current study and prior work on RIDD.

claim: Production of Hac1trunc coincides with a high-molecular weight laddering that is interpreted as ubiquitination of the truncated form.
source: Interestingly, production of Hac1trunc coincides with a high-molecular weight laddering that we interpret as ubiquitination of the truncated form.
evidence: This is stated based on immunoblot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The HAC1 mRNA is an endogenous substrate of the ribosome quality control (RQC) complex.
source: We surmise that the HAC1 mRNA is an endogenous substrate of the recently characterized ribosome quality control (RQC) complex (Brandman et al., 2012; Shen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculated based on the ubiquitination pattern observed.

claim: Hac1 initiates a major transcriptional response that re-shapes the entire ER and upregulates hundreds of target genes comprising ~5% of the genome.
source: In yeast, Hac1 initiates a major transcriptional response that re-shapes the entire ER and upregulates hundreds of target genes comprising ~5% of the genome (Travers et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Deletion of SKI2 leads to the accumulation of Hac1trunc even in the context of WT Trl1.
source: Our data show, that deletion of SKI2 leads to the accumulation of Hac1trunc – even in the context of WT Trl1.
evidence: This is stated based on immunoblot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Single cleavage by Ire1 occurs frequently and RNA decay pathways assist in degrading HAC1 mRNA fragments to prevent premature UPR signaling.
source: It is very likely that single cleavage by Ire1 occurs frequently and that RNA decay pathways assist in degrading these HAC1 mRNA fragments to prevent premature UPR signaling.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation of truncated Hac1 in ski2Δ WT cells.

claim: Tight regulation of the UPR in yeast is achieved by the interplay of several control mechanisms including RNA decay and surveillance by mRNA quality control factors.
source: We conclude that tight regulation of the UPR in yeast is achieved by the interplay of several control mechanisms to which this study adds RNA decay and surveillance by mRNA quality control factors.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the data presented.

claim: Trl1 homologs are present in all human fungal pathogens and are essential enzymes due to their role in tRNA splicing.
source: Trl1 homologs are present in all human fungal pathogens. They are essential enzymes for them due to their role in tRNA splicing.
evidence: This is stated based on knowledge of fungal biology.

claim: Trl1 homologs represent promising targets for antifungal drug discovery because their structure and mechanism are distinct from the RTCB-type tRNA ligases in metazoans.
source: They also represent promising targets for antifungal drug discovery because their structure and mechanism are distinct from the RTCB-type tRNA ligases in metazoans (as well as archaea and many bacteria).
evidence: This is stated based on the structural differences between fungal and metazoan tRNA ligases.

claim: The absence of human homologs of Trl1-LIG could be explored as a promising new drug target in antifungal therapy.
source: The absence of human homologs of Trl1-LIG could therefore be explored as a promising new drug target in antifungal therapy, whose development has largely stalled in recent years.
evidence: This is speculated based on the structural data and the lack of human homologs.

claim: The structure of Candida albicans Trl1 kinase domain Trl1-KIN was recently published.
source: Together with the recently published structure of Candida albicans Trl1 kinase domain Trl1-KIN (Remus et al., 2017), our study presents new opportunities for inhibitor screens guided by atomic-resolution Trl1 structures.
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.
